unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) and other Remittance Facilities for Residents

facts.statement: All transactions by a resident that do not alter assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India are current account transactions. Residents are free to buy or sell foreign exchange for any current account transaction except those prohibited by the Central Government, such as remittance out of lottery winnings, income from racing or riding, purchase of lottery tickets, banned or proscribed magazines, football pools or sweepstakes. Other transactions are capital account transactions.
facts.locator: Introduction; S03 printed p. 47 gives matching examples

facts.statement: Under the LRS all resident individuals, including minors, may freely remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year (April-March) for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both. A minor's declaration form is countersigned by the natural guardian. The scheme is not available to corporates, partnership firms, HUFs, trusts and similar entities.
facts.locator: Q1; S03 printed p. 47 adds that NRIs are not eligible

facts.statement: There is no restriction on the frequency of remittances, but the total foreign exchange purchased or remitted through all sources in India in a financial year must stay within USD 2,50,000. Once USD 2,50,000 has been remitted in the year, no further remittance is allowed under the scheme, even if the proceeds of the investments are brought back to India.

The scheme is not available for remittances prohibited under Schedule I or restricted under Schedule II of the Current Account Transactions Rules, remittances for margins or margin calls to overseas exchanges or counterparties, purchase of FCCBs issued by Indian companies in the overseas secondary market, trading in foreign exchange abroad, capital account remittances to countries identified by the FATF as non-cooperative, remittances to individuals and entities identified as posing a significant risk of terrorism, and gifting by a resident to another resident in foreign currency for credit to the latter's foreign currency account abroad.
facts.locator: Q2; S03 pp. 48-50 lists the same

facts.statement: Purposes within the USD 2,50,000 limit include private visits to any country except Nepal and Bhutan, gift or donation, going abroad for employment, emigration, maintenance of close relatives abroad, travel for business, conferences or specialised training, medical expenses and attending to a patient, studies abroad, and any other current account transaction not otherwise defined as current account in FEMA.

The remitter must give a PAN for all LRS transactions through authorised persons, irrespective of the amount; the authorised dealer is guided by the purpose declared in Form A2, and the ultimate responsibility for compliance is the remitter's. Remittances may be made in any freely convertible foreign currency.

For capital account remittances the individual designates a branch of an authorised dealer through which all such remittances are made, and should have maintained an account with the bank for at least one year before the remittance; a new customer is subject to due diligence on the account and the source of funds. These conditions are not applied to current account transactions. LRS does not allow banks to extend fund-based or non-fund-based facilities to enable capital account remittances, though they may do so for current account remittances. A bank cannot open foreign currency accounts in India for residents under the scheme. No prior approval is needed to open and hold a foreign currency account abroad for LRS remittances.
facts.locator: Q10, Q12, Q16, Q17, Q23; S03 p. 55 agrees on the designated branch and the one-year requirement

facts.statement: The investor can retain and reinvest income earned on investments made under the scheme, but received, realised, unspent or unused foreign exchange, unless reinvested, must be repatriated and surrendered to an authorised person within 180 days from the date of receipt, realisation, purchase or acquisition, or the date of return to India.
facts.locator: Q4; S03 p. 56 states the same 180 days

facts.statement: Remittances under the scheme can be consolidated for family members if each complies with the scheme's terms, but clubbing for capital account transactions such as opening a bank account or investment is not allowed unless the other family members are co-owners or co-partners of the investment or account. A sole proprietor and the proprietorship are one: if the proprietor has remitted USD 2,50,000 in his own capacity he cannot remit another USD 2,50,000 as owner of the business.
facts.locator: Q5, Q22; S03 p. 55 agrees on the co-owner condition

facts.statement: A resident individual may make a rupee loan to an NRI or PIO who is a close relative (as defined in section 2(77) of the Companies Act, 2013) if the loan is interest-free with minimum maturity of one year, within the USD 2,50,000 limit, used for the borrower's personal needs or business in India (not chit fund or Nidhi business, agricultural or plantation activity, real estate business, farm houses or TDR trading), credited to the borrower's NRO account, not remitted abroad, and repaid by inward remittance or debit to an NRO, NRE or FCNR account or from sale proceeds of the asset against which it was granted. A rupee gift to such a relative may likewise be credited to the NRO account within the same limit.
facts.locator: Q25 and Q26; S03 p. 57 agrees on the loan conditions

payload.title: Current or capital: does it change what you own abroad?
payload.core_explanation_md:
FEMA sorts every foreign exchange transaction into two boxes. The test is one question: **does the transaction change the resident's assets or liabilities outside India?**

- **No change: current account.** Paying a child's tuition abroad, family maintenance, a holiday, medical treatment. Residents may buy or sell foreign exchange for these freely, except for the few purposes the Central Government has prohibited (lottery winnings, lottery tickets, racing income, banned magazines, football pools and sweepstakes).
- **A change: capital account.** Buying shares abroad creates an asset outside India; buying a property abroad does the same; opening a foreign bank account does too. These are allowed only as the rules permit and up to the limits they set.

The LRS is the window that lets a resident individual do **either kind, or both**, up to one annual ceiling.

payload.title: The LRS in one view
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Who**: any resident individual, **minors included** (the natural guardian countersigns). Not companies, firms, HUFs or trusts.

**How much**: up to **USD 2,50,000 per financial year** (April to March), for current account, capital account, or a mix.

**How often**: as often as you like. What counts is the **cumulative total** for the year from all sources in India.

**The one-way gate**: once USD 2,50,000 has been used, no more remittances under the scheme that year, **even if the money from your investments has come back to India**.

**Paperwork**: PAN for every transaction whatever the amount; the purpose is declared in **Form A2**; the bank is guided by that declaration, but the **remitter is ultimately responsible** for compliance. Any freely convertible currency may be remitted.

payload.title: What the LRS will not pay for
payload.core_explanation_md:
Some remittances are out of bounds even inside the USD 2,50,000 limit:

- anything **prohibited** (Schedule I) or **restricted** (Schedule II) in the current account rules, such as lottery tickets
- **margins or margin calls** to overseas exchanges or counterparties
- buying **FCCBs** issued by Indian companies in the overseas secondary market
- **trading in foreign exchange** abroad
- capital account remittances to countries the **FATF** has identified as non-cooperative
- remittances to individuals or entities flagged as posing **significant terrorism risk**
- **gifting in foreign currency** by one resident to another, for the credit of the latter's foreign currency account abroad

A simple way to remember the pattern: speculation on exchange or margin, anything illegal at home, and anything touching sanctioned or high-risk destinations.

payload.title: Where the money may go: permitted purposes
payload.core_explanation_md:
Within the annual limit, a resident individual may remit for:

- **Travel**: private visits to any country except **Nepal and Bhutan**; business trips, conferences, specialised training
- **People**: gifts or donations, maintenance of close relatives abroad, emigration, going abroad for employment
- **Health**: medical treatment, check-ups, or accompanying a patient
- **Education**: studies abroad
- **Anything else** that is a current account transaction not otherwise defined as one in FEMA, which the bank may process without RBI permission if it is not prohibited or restricted and is genuine

Capital account uses such as investing abroad or buying property abroad are also allowed within the same limit.

self_check.prompt_text: A resident wants to send money for a holiday in Bhutan and for a month-long course in Singapore. Which of the two is a permitted purpose under the LRS?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Singapore course. Private visits to Nepal and Bhutan are excluded from the facility.

payload.title: Capital account remittances: extra conditions
payload.core_explanation_md:
Sending money abroad to **invest or hold assets** brings extra conditions that current account remittances do not carry:

- **Designate one branch** of an authorised dealer through which all capital account remittances go.
- **One-year relationship**: the account with that bank should be at least a year old; a new customer faces due diligence on the account and source of funds.
- **No borrowed money**: banks may not lend, fund-based or non-fund-based, to help a resident make a capital account remittance under the LRS. They may do so for current account remittances.
- **Bring back what is not used**: unspent or unused foreign exchange must be surrendered to an authorised person within **180 days** of receipt, realisation, purchase, acquisition or return to India, unless reinvested. Income earned on the investments may be retained and reinvested.
- **Foreign currency account**: no prior approval is needed to open one abroad. Banks in India cannot open foreign currency accounts for residents under the LRS.

payload.title: Families and the sole proprietor: who shares the limit?
payload.core_explanation_md:
Two situations often catch candidates out.

**Family members.** Each resident individual has **his or her own** USD 2,50,000. Remittances can be **consolidated** across family members, but for a capital account transaction (opening a bank account, investing), another family member's limit **cannot be clubbed in** unless that person is a **co-owner or co-partner** of the investment or account.

**The sole proprietor.** A sole proprietorship has **no legal existence apart from its owner**. If the proprietor remits USD 2,50,000 in his own name, the same proprietor cannot remit a second USD 2,50,000 by debiting the business's current account. The eligibility used is the **individual's**.

payload.title: A rupee gift or loan to a close relative who is an NRI
payload.core_explanation_md:
A resident can send rupees (not foreign currency) to a close relative who is an **NRI or PIO**.

**Gift**: by crossed cheque or electronic transfer; credited to the relative's **NRO account**; counted within the giver's USD 2,50,000.

**Loan**, all of these together:
- **interest-free**, **minimum one year**
- within the lender's USD 2,50,000
- used for the borrower's **personal needs or own business in India**, never for chit fund or Nidhi business, agricultural or plantation activity, real estate business, farm houses or TDR trading
- **credited to the NRO account**; **not remitted abroad**
- repaid by inward remittance, or by debit to an **NRO, NRE or FCNR** account, or from the sale proceeds of the asset against which the loan was granted

"Close relative" means a relative as defined in section 2(77) of the Companies Act, 2013.

payload.title: How much headroom is left in the year?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a resident individual remits USD 80,000 for a child's studies abroad in June, USD 55,000 as a gift to a relative in September, and USD 40,000 to buy shares abroad in December. In February her sole proprietorship asks to remit USD 90,000 from its current account to a supplier's relative abroad for a gift. Does the scheme allow it?

worked_steps.description: State the annual ceiling for an individual.
Add the three remittances made in her own name.
A sole proprietorship has no legal existence apart from the proprietor, so the firm's request counts against her own limit. Compare the request with the headroom.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Not as asked: only USD 75,000 of headroom is left, so USD 90,000 would exceed the limit by USD 15,000; anything above needs RBI approval

self_check.prompt_text: What if she had separately remitted USD 75,000 from the proprietorship earlier in the same year, believing the firm had its own limit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It would still count: the firm and the proprietor are one, so her total would be USD 250,000 and nothing more could go.

payload.stem_md: A resident individual has remitted USD 2,50,000 under the LRS in a financial year for investment abroad. Later in the same year the investment proceeds are brought back to India. Can she make a further remittance under the scheme that year?

options.text_md: Yes: the returned amount restores her limit
options.explanation_md: Returned proceeds do not restore the limit.

options.text_md: No: once USD 2,50,000 has been remitted, no further remittance is allowed that year, even if the proceeds come back
options.explanation_md: The limit is cumulative for the financial year and is not restored by money coming back.

options.text_md: Yes, but only for current account purposes
options.explanation_md: No further remittance is allowed under the scheme for either kind.

options.text_md: Yes, after one month
options.explanation_md: There is no waiting-period rule that restores the limit.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The limit is cumulative for the financial year. Once USD 2,50,000 has been remitted, no further remittance is allowed under the scheme that year, even if proceeds of the investments have been brought back to India.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following remittances is NOT allowed under the LRS?

options.text_md: Sending funds as margin to an overseas exchange
options.explanation_md: Margins or margin calls to overseas exchanges or counterparties are excluded.

options.text_md: Paying fees for a course abroad
options.explanation_md: Studies abroad is a permitted purpose.

options.text_md: Maintaining a close relative living abroad
options.explanation_md: Maintenance of close relatives abroad is a permitted purpose.

options.text_md: Paying for medical treatment abroad
options.explanation_md: Medical treatment abroad is a permitted purpose.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Remittance for margins or margin calls to overseas exchanges or counterparties is not available under the scheme. The other three are permitted purposes.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is eligible to remit foreign exchange under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme?

options.text_md: A private limited company
options.explanation_md: The scheme is not available to corporates.

options.text_md: A partnership firm
options.explanation_md: The scheme is not available to partnership firms.

options.text_md: A Hindu undivided family
options.explanation_md: The scheme is not available to HUFs.

options.text_md: A minor resident in India, with the natural guardian countersigning the declaration
options.explanation_md: Resident individuals, including minors, are eligible.

payload.correct_explanation_md: All resident individuals, including minors, are eligible; for a minor the natural guardian countersigns the declaration. Companies, firms, HUFs and trusts are not.

payload.stem_md: A resident individual remits USD 65,000 for studies abroad in May, USD 48,000 for maintenance of a close relative in August and USD 72,000 to buy foreign shares in November, all in one financial year (illustrative figures). How many US dollars can she still remit under the LRS in that year?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give a whole number of US dollars.

payload.stem_md: A resident individual invests in shares of an overseas company and the shares are allotted in her name. How is this transaction classified under FEMA?

options.text_md: Current account transaction, because it is an ordinary payment
options.explanation_md: A current account transaction does not alter assets or liabilities outside India.

options.text_md: Neither, because it falls under the LRS only
options.explanation_md: The LRS covers both current and capital account transactions; it does not replace the classification.

options.text_md: Capital account transaction, because it creates an asset outside India
options.explanation_md: It alters the resident's assets outside India.

options.text_md: A prohibited transaction under Schedule I
options.explanation_md: It is permitted within the scheme's limit and conditions.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A transaction that creates an asset outside India is a capital account transaction. Current account transactions do not alter assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India.

payload.stem_md: What does the Reserve Bank require about the Permanent Account Number (PAN) for LRS remittances through authorised persons?

options.text_md: PAN is needed only above USD 25,000
options.explanation_md: There is no such threshold.

options.text_md: PAN is mandatory for all LRS transactions, whatever the amount
options.explanation_md: PAN must be provided for all transactions under the scheme.

options.text_md: PAN is needed only for capital account remittances
options.explanation_md: It is needed for all transactions.

options.text_md: PAN is not needed if Form A2 is filed
options.explanation_md: Form A2 states the purpose; it does not replace PAN.

payload.correct_explanation_md: It is mandatory for the resident individual to provide the PAN for all transactions under the LRS made through authorised persons.

payload.stem_md: In which currency may a remittance under the LRS be made?

options.text_md: Only US dollars
options.explanation_md: The limit is stated in US dollars but remittances can be in any freely convertible currency.

options.text_md: Only the currency of the country where the money is going
options.explanation_md: No such restriction applies.

options.text_md: Only Indian rupees
options.explanation_md: The scheme concerns foreign exchange.

options.text_md: Any freely convertible foreign currency
options.explanation_md: Remittances are not limited to US dollars.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Remittances can be made in any freely convertible foreign currency; the USD 2,50,000 is a measure of the limit.

payload.stem_md: Which statement about capital account remittances under the LRS is correct?

options.text_md: The bank may not extend fund-based or non-fund-based facilities to help the resident make the remittance
options.explanation_md: LRS does not envisage credit facilities to facilitate capital account remittances.

options.text_md: The bank may lend freely to fund the remittance if the loan is secured
options.explanation_md: Credit facilities for capital account remittances are not envisaged.

options.text_md: Any branch of any bank may be used for each remittance
options.explanation_md: The individual designates one branch for all capital account remittances.

options.text_md: A new account may be used immediately without any history
options.explanation_md: The account should have been maintained for at least a year, and a new customer faces due diligence.

payload.correct_explanation_md: LRS does not allow banks to extend fund-based or non-fund-based facilities to facilitate capital account remittances, though they may do so for current account remittances.

payload.stem_md: A resident individual has already remitted USD 2,50,000 in her own name under the LRS in a financial year. Her sole proprietorship now wants to remit another USD 2,50,000 by debiting its current account. What is the position?

options.text_md: Allowed: the firm has its own USD 2,50,000 limit
options.explanation_md: A sole proprietorship has no separate limit.

options.text_md: Allowed, if the firm has a PAN of its own
options.explanation_md: A separate PAN does not create a separate limit.

options.text_md: Not allowed: the owner and the proprietorship are the same person, so the individual's limit has been used
options.explanation_md: There is no legal distinction between the proprietor and a sole proprietorship.

options.text_md: Allowed, but only for current account purposes
options.explanation_md: The limit is the individual's and is used up.

payload.correct_explanation_md: In a sole proprietorship there is no legal distinction between owner and business, so the eligibility used is the individual's and a second USD 2,50,000 cannot be remitted.

payload.stem_md: A resident individual lends rupees to her brother, an NRI. Which condition must the loan meet?

options.text_md: It may carry interest at the market rate
options.explanation_md: The loan must be interest-free.

options.text_md: It must be interest-free, with a minimum maturity of one year, and be credited to his NRO account
options.explanation_md: These are among the conditions of the facility.

options.text_md: It may be repaid within a week
options.explanation_md: The minimum maturity is one year.

options.text_md: It may be credited directly to his NRE account
options.explanation_md: It should be credited to the NRO account.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The loan must be free of interest, have a minimum maturity of one year, be within the lender's LRS limit, be used for permitted purposes in India and be credited to the NRO account of the NRI or PIO.

payload.stem_md: A resident individual remitted funds abroad under the LRS but did not use all of the foreign exchange. Within how many days of receipt, realisation, purchase or acquisition must unused foreign exchange be repatriated and surrendered to an authorised person, unless it is reinvested?

options.text_md: 30 days
options.explanation_md: No such 30-day rule applies to unspent foreign exchange.

options.text_md: 60 days
options.explanation_md: 60 days is not the period for unspent foreign exchange.

options.text_md: 365 days
options.explanation_md: The period is shorter.

options.text_md: 180 days
options.explanation_md: This is the period stated.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Unless reinvested, received, realised, unspent or unused foreign exchange must be repatriated and surrendered within 180 days.

unresolved: TCS on LRS remittances (LO_05) is in batch BFM-A-U02-B002; the courseware (printed pp. 53-54) describes the 2020 rules (5% above Rs 7 lakh), which are superseded.

Reporting requirements (LO_06): the courseware (printed pp. 55-57, 57-58) covers the ODI forms (Form ODI Part I and II, APRs, 30-day and 60-day rules) under the 2004 Regulations that were replaced by the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, and daily XBRL reporting by banks; neither is taught until checked against current RBI sources.

The courseware states a cash cap of Rs 50,000 for private visits and foreign currency note limits by destination (printed p. 51); these are not taught until checked against the current RBI Master Direction.
The FEMA section descriptions (printed pp. 47-48: sections 4, 6, 10(6), 11, 13) and penalty amounts are not taught: India Code could not be checked.
The RBI LRS FAQ used is dated 6 April 2023; no later change to the USD 2,50,000 limit or the scheme conditions was found, but RBI could have issued notices not seen.
